title: Networking & Protocols
summary: Every service you deploy communicates over a network. Understanding the OSI model, TCP/IP, HTTP, and DNS is not theoretical — it directly determines how you debug connection failures, design service meshes, and secure traffic.

sections.title: The OSI model and TCP/IP in practice
sections.body:
The OSI model is a conceptual framework that describes how network communication works in 7 layers. In practice, DevOps engineers care about layers 3–7.

```
Layer 7 — Application   HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH, SMTP, gRPC
Layer 6 — Presentation  TLS/SSL encryption, encoding
Layer 5 — Session       Connection management, sessions
Layer 4 — Transport     TCP (reliable), UDP (fast)
Layer 3 — Network       IP addressing, routing
Layer 2 — Data Link     MAC addresses, Ethernet, ARP
Layer 1 — Physical      Cables, radio signals
```

**Where you spend your time:**
- **L7**: HTTP status codes, headers, timeouts, TLS certificates
- **L4**: TCP connection refused vs timeout (is the port open? is the process listening?)
- **L3**: Routing issues, VPC subnets, security group rules

**TCP vs UDP:**

```
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
  ✓ Reliable — guarantees delivery, retransmits lost packets
  ✓ Ordered — packets arrive in order
  ✓ Connection-oriented — 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK)
  ✗ Higher overhead
  Used for: HTTP/S, SSH, database connections

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
  ✓ Fast — no connection overhead, no retransmit
  ✗ Unreliable — packets may drop or arrive out of order
  Used for: DNS queries, video streaming, game traffic
```

**Ports you must know:**

```
22    SSH
53    DNS (UDP/TCP)
80    HTTP
443   HTTPS
3306  MySQL
5432  PostgreSQL
6379  Redis
6443  Kubernetes API server
8080  Common dev/alt HTTP
```

```bash
# Check if a port is open on a remote host
nc -zv 10.0.0.1 443        # TCP
# Connection to 10.0.0.1 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!

# See what's listening locally
ss -tlnp | grep ':443'
```

sections.title: HTTP and HTTPS: how the web actually works
sections.body:
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the protocol powering every REST API, web app, and webhook you'll work with.

**Request structure:**
```
GET /api/pods?namespace=default HTTP/1.1
Host: k8s-api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
```

**Response structure:**
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
X-Request-Id: abc-123

{"items": [...]}
```

**HTTP methods:**
```
GET     — read a resource (idempotent, no side effects)
POST    — create a resource
PUT     — replace a resource entirely
PATCH   — update part of a resource
DELETE  — delete a resource
HEAD    — like GET but no body (check if resource exists)
```

**Status codes:**
```
2xx — Success
  200 OK           — request succeeded
  201 Created      — resource was created
  204 No Content   — success, no body

3xx — Redirect
  301 Moved Permanently
  302 Found (temporary redirect)

4xx — Client error
  400 Bad Request  — malformed input
  401 Unauthorized — missing/invalid authentication
  403 Forbidden    — authenticated but not authorized
  404 Not Found    — resource doesn't exist
  409 Conflict     — state conflict (e.g. already exists)
  422 Unprocessable Entity — validation failed
  429 Too Many Requests — rate limited

5xx — Server error
  500 Internal Server Error — bug in the server
  502 Bad Gateway           — upstream server returned invalid response
  503 Service Unavailable   — service down or overloaded
  504 Gateway Timeout       — upstream didn't respond in time
```

```bash
# Inspect HTTP responses
curl -I https://kubernetes.io/docs/   # headers only
curl -v https://httpbin.org/get       # verbose: full exchange
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com  # just status

# Follow redirects (-L), ignore TLS errors (-k), set timeout
curl -Lk --max-time 10 http://service.local/health
```

sections.title: DNS: the internet's phonebook
sections.body:
DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable names to IP addresses. Most connectivity issues in distributed systems come down to DNS.

**How DNS resolution works:**

```
browser asks: "what is the IP for api.example.com?"

1. Check /etc/hosts (local override)
2. Check local DNS cache
3. Query DNS resolver (configured in /etc/resolv.conf)
4. Resolver checks cache — if not found:
5. Resolver queries root nameservers (.) → which TLD server handles .com?
6. Queries .com TLD nameservers → which NS handles example.com?
7. Queries example.com nameservers → what is api.example.com?
8. Returns A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6)
```

**DNS record types:**
```
A        maps hostname to IPv4 address
AAAA     maps hostname to IPv6 address
CNAME    alias from one hostname to another
MX       mail server for a domain
TXT      arbitrary text (used for SPF, DMARC, verification)
NS       nameservers for a domain
SRV      service location record (used by Kubernetes)
PTR      reverse DNS (IP → hostname)
```

```bash
# Query DNS
dig google.com                     # full response
dig google.com A                   # just A records
dig google.com MX                  # mail records
dig +short google.com              # just the IP
dig @8.8.8.8 google.com            # query specific resolver (8.8.8.8 = Google)

# Trace the full resolution chain
dig +trace google.com

# Reverse lookup (IP → hostname)
dig -x 8.8.8.8

# Check DNS in Kubernetes
# CoreDNS runs inside the cluster and resolves service names
# Service DNS format: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
dig @10.96.0.10 argocd-server.argocd.svc.cluster.local

# /etc/resolv.conf defines where to send DNS queries
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# /etc/hosts takes priority over DNS
cat /etc/hosts
```

**Kubernetes DNS pattern:**
```
Service name:       web-app
Full DNS name:      web-app.default.svc.cluster.local
From same ns:       web-app
From other ns:      web-app.default
Cross-cluster:      web-app.default.svc.cluster.local
```

sections.title: Firewalls, security groups, and network policies
sections.body:
A firewall controls which traffic is allowed to reach a network or host. In cloud environments, this is usually called a 'security group' or 'network ACL'.

```bash
# ── iptables (Linux firewall) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# View current rules
iptables -L -n -v

# Allow incoming SSH
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Allow incoming HTTP/S
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

# Drop everything else incoming
iptables -A INPUT -j DROP

# ── ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall — Ubuntu wrapper around iptables) ─────────
ufw status
ufw allow 22/tcp
ufw allow 80/tcp
ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432  # only internal IPs to postgres
ufw enable

# ── AWS Security Groups ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Security groups are stateful: if you allow outbound, inbound response is auto-allowed
# Common mistake: allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 (should use VPN or bastion)

# ── Kubernetes Network Policies ──────────────────────────────────────────
# By default, all pods can talk to all other pods
# Network Policies restrict traffic at the pod level
```

```yaml
# Allow only traffic from pods with label app=frontend to app=backend
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
```

```bash
# In the sandbox: apply and inspect network policies
kubectl get networkpolicies -A

# Test connectivity between pods
kubectl exec -it deploy/web-app -- wget -qO- http://argocd-server.argocd:80/healthz
```

sections.title: Exercise: network debugging in the sandbox
sections.body:
Use networking tools to map out and verify the sandbox cluster's network topology.

```bash
# 1. DNS resolution inside the cluster
# Find the CoreDNS service IP
kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system

# Query it to resolve service names
kubectl run -it --rm dns-test --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup argocd-server.argocd.svc.cluster.local

# 2. Inspect pod networking
kubectl get pods -A -o wide    # shows IP of each pod

# 3. Check what ports the ArgoCD server is listening on
kubectl exec -n argocd deploy/argocd-server -- ss -tlnp

# 4. Test HTTP connectivity to the backend API
curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/cluster/status | python3 -m json.tool

# 5. Trace what happens when you hit the k3s API
curl -v -k https://k3s:6443/version 2>&1 | grep -E '^[<>*]'
# Notice: TLS connection, then HTTP/2, then JSON response

# 6. Find all services and their cluster IPs
kubectl get svc -A -o wide

# 7. Check the Kubernetes DNS config in a pod
kubectl exec deploy/web-app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Should show: nameserver 10.96.0.10 (CoreDNS)

# 8. HTTP status code challenge — what does each return?
for url in \
  'http://localhost:8000/api/lessons' \
  'http://localhost:8000/api/lessons/does-not-exist' \
  'http://localhost:8000/nonexistent'; do
  status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$url")
  echo "$status $url"
done
```
